title: From Adam to Noah
overview: A family line runs ten generations from Adam to Noah, giving each man's age when his son was born and when he died, though Enoch's entry ends differently and Noah's story is left open for the chapters ahead.

parts.label: Made in God's likeness (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The list opens by echoing Genesis 1: God made humans, male and female, in his likeness and blessed them. The Hebrew word adam means a human being or humankind, which is why one translation has God naming them Mankind and the other has Adam; either way the name covers both the man and the woman.

parts.label: Seth in Adam's likeness (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: Seth is born in Adam's own likeness and image, the same pair of words used when God made humans, which suggests God's image carries on through children. Some Christian readers, especially in traditions that stress inherited sin, also see a damaged human nature being passed down here, while others see only family resemblance.

parts.label: Long lives, same ending (vv. 5-20)
parts.note: Each entry follows the same pattern and ends by noting that the man died, a steady reminder that the death announced in Genesis 3 reaches everyone. No one knows for sure why the ages are so huge: some read them literally, some as symbolic, and scholars note that ancient Mesopotamian king lists also gave early rulers enormously long reigns.

parts.label: Enoch walked with God (vv. 21-24)
parts.note: Enoch, seventh from Adam, walked with God (one translation adds 'faithfully'), a phrase for a close, ongoing relationship. Rather than saying he died, the text says God took him: the letter to the Hebrews (11:5) and many ancient Jewish writings read this as being taken without dying, while some later Jewish interpreters read it as an early death.

parts.label: Methuselah's long life (vv. 25-27)
parts.note: Methuselah lives 969 years, the longest life in the Bible, yet his entry still ends with his death. By the numbers in the standard Hebrew text he dies in the year the flood begins (compare 7:6), though the text never says how, and some ancient Greek copies give different figures.

parts.label: Lamech's hope for Noah (vv. 28-32)
parts.note: Lamech, a different man from the violent Lamech of chapter 4, names his son Noah, a name that sounds like the Hebrew word for rest, hoping for relief from farming the ground the LORD cursed. The list stops with Noah's three sons, setting up the flood story, and Christians read it alongside Luke 3, which traces Jesus' family line back through these names to Adam.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether these ages are exact history that can be added up to date the world, as some have done, or a stylized family record whose large numbers make a point rather than give a timeline.
think: Most people in this list are remembered only by their years and their children; what do you think such a short record would miss about a life?
